stem: http_requests_total has labels job, instance, method and code. What labels does the result of sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) have?

options.note: Right. by keeps only the listed labels.
That would be without (instance). by keeps only what you list.
With by (job), the job label is preserved.
Aggregation always removes some dimensions. Here everything except job goes.

explanation: by drops labels that aren't listed in the by clause. without does the opposite and removes only the listed labels.

stem: Same metric (labels job, instance, method, code). What labels does sum without (instance) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) keep?

options.note: Right. without removes only the listed label and keeps the rest.
Reversed. without removes instance.
That's what by (job) would give.
Only instance is removed.

explanation: without removes the listed labels from the result, while all other labels are preserved.

stem: memory_consumption_bytes fans out by application, instance and group. Which expression is equivalent to sum without (instance) (memory_consumption_bytes)?

options.note: Right. Removing instance leaves application and group, which is exactly what by (application, group) keeps.
That keeps instance, the opposite.
That collapses everything to a single series.
That keeps only instance.

explanation: From the docs' sum example: sum without (instance) (memory_consumption_bytes) is equivalent to sum by (application, group) (memory_consumption_bytes).
hint: List what's left after removing instance.

options.text: A single series with no labels: the total across all series
options.note: Right. Without by or without, aggregation runs over all label dimensions.
You'd need by (instance) for that.
sum always combines series.

options.text: An error, because a by clause is required
options.note: by and without are optional.

explanation: Aggregation operators can aggregate over all label dimensions, or preserve distinct dimensions with a without or by clause. With neither, everything is combined.

stem: Which of these are valid and equivalent? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. The clause before the expression.
Right. The clause after the expression is also valid.
The clause can't go inside the parentheses, attached to the argument.
The clause comes after the operator name or after the expression, never before the operator.

explanation: The without or by clause may be used before or after the expression: <aggr-op> [by|without (labels)] (expr) or <aggr-op>(expr) [by|without (labels)].

stem: You need the total per-second request rate per job. Which expression follows the docs' guidance?

options.note: Right. rate first, so each series' counter resets are handled, then sum.
Summing raw counters first hides each series' resets, so rate can't detect them.
That's the sum of raw counters, not a rate.
irate needs a range vector, and the docs recommend rate for this kind of total.

explanation: When combining rate() with an aggregation operator, always take rate() first, then aggregate. Otherwise rate() can't detect counter resets.

options.text: The 5 series with the highest values, with their original labels
options.note: Right. topk returns a subset of the input series, labels intact.

options.text: A single series whose value is the sum of the top 5
options.note: topk doesn't combine values. It selects series.

options.text: The top 5 values with all labels removed
options.note: Original labels are kept.
It returns all of the top k series.

explanation: topk and bottomk differ from other aggregators: they return a subset of k values from the input samples, including the original labels.
hint: It's a filter, not a calculation.

stem: In topk(3, sum by (app, proc) (rate(instance_cpu_time_ns[5m]))), what is returned?

options.text: The 3 app/proc combinations using the most CPU
options.note: Right. The inner sum gives one series per app/proc, and topk picks the top 3 of those.

options.text: The top 3 instances within each app
options.note: topk here isn't grouped. It applies to the summed series overall.

options.text: The total CPU of the top 3 apps added together
options.note: topk returns series. It doesn't add them.
Only 3 are returned.

explanation: This is the docs' example for getting the top 3 CPU users grouped by application and process type.

stem: In topk by (job) (2, x), what role does by (job) play?

options.text: It defines groups: you get the top 2 series within each job, with original labels
options.note: Right. For topk and bottomk, by and without only bucket the input.

options.text: It removes every label except job from the output
options.note: That's what by does for sum or avg. topk keeps the original labels.

options.text: It sorts the result by job name
options.note: It groups. It doesn't define sort order.

options.text: It's invalid, because topk doesn't accept by
options.note: topk accepts by and without.

explanation: For topk and bottomk, by and without are only used to bucket the input vector. The returned series keep their labels.
hint: topk is different from other aggregators.

stem: Assuming one series per running instance, how do you count running instances per application?

options.note: Right. count counts the series in each app group.
That adds up CPU time values. It doesn't count instances.
count_values groups by sample value, not by an existing label.
That counts samples over time per series, not series per app.

explanation: count(v) counts the number of elements in the vector. The examples page uses count by (app) (instance_cpu_time_ns) for exactly this.
hint: You want the number of series, not their values.

options.text: One series per distinct value of build_version, labelled version=<value>, counting how many series had that value
options.note: Right. That's the docs' example for counting binaries per build version.

options.text: The number of distinct label values called version
options.note: It looks at sample values, not existing label values.

options.text: The sum of all build_version values
options.note: It counts. It doesn't sum.
It returns a series for every distinct value.

explanation: count_values(l, v) outputs one series per unique sample value in v. Each has an additional label l whose value is that sample value, and its value is how many times it occurred.

stem: What's the difference between quantile(0.9, x) and quantile_over_time(0.9, x[1h])?

options.text: quantile works across series at one instant; quantile_over_time works across one series' samples over time
options.note: Right. Aggregation operators work across dimensions; _over_time functions work across time.
They aggregate along different axes.

options.text: quantile works over time; quantile_over_time works across series
options.note: Reversed.
quantile is a general aggregation operator over float samples.

explanation: quantile(φ, v) calculates the φ-quantile over dimensions, across series. quantile_over_time calculates it over the samples in each series' window.
hint: One works across the spreadsheet's rows, the other down its time axis.

stem: When writing recording rules that aggregate, which clause does the best-practices guide recommend, and why?

options.text: without, listing the labels you're removing, so other useful labels such as job are kept
options.note: Right. That avoids conflicts and gives more useful metrics and alerts.

options.text: by, listing only job, so results stay small
options.note: The guide recommends without, to preserve other labels.

options.text: Neither. Always aggregate to a single series
options.note: That throws away useful dimensions.
That isn't the guide's advice.

explanation: Always specify a without clause with the labels you're aggregating away. This preserves all other labels such as job, which avoids conflicts and gives more useful metrics and alerts.
hint: Which clause automatically keeps labels you didn't think about?
